originality.rationale: The same Fibonacci–Thue–Morse sign word is classical, but the compared papers study complexity, correlations, asymptotic digit-sum laws or orthogonality rather than a three-class exact signed cutoff formula with sharp growth exponent. Existing binary Newman phenomena are not logical covers of a distinct Zeckendorf weighted numeration. Public exact-record search returned fixed-weight Zeckendorf slice counts and binary Newman sums, neither implying the claimed unbounded parity-weighted three-class biases.
residual_risks: An equivalent formula could exist in unindexed automatic-sequence or numeration-system literature; search failures do not prove uniqueness.

Some later pages of the Drmota–Steiner paper and the primary 1969 Newman article were not inspected in full. Their checked statements use materially different statistics; priority nevertheless merits independent verification.
The exponent sharpness is established only for Fibonacci cutoffs, not for all integer cutoffs.

value.rationale: The exact conditional sign imbalance is a natural invariant of a classical digit-parity sequence. It exposes a permanent positive bias in multiples of three and simultaneous negative biases in two other classes while their global signed sum remains bounded. The sharp positive exponent log(4+sqrt(15))/(8 log(phi))=0.536... distinguishes a genuine super-square-root arithmetic phenomenon not supplied by word complexity or digit-sum central-limit statements. It applies to infinitely many canonically defined Fibonacci cutoffs and is not a routine finite computation.
